The current government's term has nearly a year left. After lawmakers returned from a "study and exchange visit" to Beijing, Chief Executive John Lee today (the 28th) held his first "dialogue exchange session," conducted behind closed doors in the Legislative Council banquet hall, lasting about 1.5 hours. After the meeting, the Chief Executive and Legislative Council President Starry Lee met the media. Lee said that an unrestricted, "warm and in-depth" exchange was held with 67 lawmakers to strengthen consensus, comparing them to "members of Team Hong Kong." She also noted that the executive and legislative branches are "in the same boat," and that the Legislative Council is a partner of the government in governing Hong Kong and pursuing reform: "We are all Team Hong Kong."

Chief Executive John Lee and Legislative Council President Starry Lee met the media after the dialogue exchange session concluded.

After the "dialogue exchange session," Chief Executive John Lee and Legislative Council President Starry Lee met reporters. Lee said he held warm, in-depth exchanges with 67 lawmakers to enhance mutual understanding, narrow distances, and shared his thoughts on "patriots governing Hong Kong." Lee noted that he regards the Legislative Council as a reform partner of the government, with the executive and legislative branches sharing the same goal of solving problems for the public. Through dialogue and exchange, different perspectives can be connected, and by putting themselves in others' shoes, the two sides can both check and balance and complement each other, helping promote consensus between the executive and legislative branches and focus more on getting things done.

Lee continued, saying that under executive-led governance, he often thinks about how to continuously create new value for "patriots governing Hong Kong." This dialogue is one such innovative initiative. In a relaxed environment, without the constraints of meeting rules, "the Chief Executive and lawmakers chatted just like members of a Team Hong Kong," discussing issues without restrictions, in a warm and in-depth manner. The discussions were not limited to one-on-one, but could involve in-depth discussions on the same topic with multiple lawmakers at the same time, sharing journeys and feelings, adding a human touch to communication.

Lee said that without any meeting rules, he held warm and in-depth discussions with lawmakers.

Lee also spoke at length about his thoughts on "patriots governing Hong Kong," noting that driving reform will upset many vested interests, and finding solutions is not easy. The executive and legislative branches must handle systemic relationships—including micro and macro, comprehensive and partial, immediate and long-term, special and general, primary and secondary—to achieve high-level consensus and get things done. Lee described today's exchange as positive and constructive, saying experience will be summarized to review room for optimization. He also mentioned hearing lawmakers' accounts of their Beijing study visit, believing that national policies and implementation details are worth referencing.

Lee said the exchange session was very successful, one outcome being that lawmakers, drawing on Beijing's 12345 hotline, proposed visiting the 1823 service, a suggestion the Chief Executive acknowledged and agreed to.

Starry Lee: Very successful, no topic off-limits

Starry Lee described the exchange session as very successful, noting the Chief Executive and lawmakers interacted in a relaxed and candid atmosphere, with 15 lawmakers expressing their views and speaking, "covering virtually everything." She described the executive and legislative branches as "in the same boat," with the Legislative Council serving as the government's partner in governing Hong Kong and pursuing reform: "We are all Team Hong Kong." She expressed confidence that as long as the executive and legislative branches continue to maintain positive interaction and efficient collaboration through different channels, adhere to a people-oriented approach with the people as the top priority, and learn more from the country's successful experience, they will be even better able to resolve issues for the public.

She also noted that the 15 lawmakers who spoke shared their "study outcomes" from Beijing. Several lawmakers had earlier visited Beijing's "12345" Citizens' Hotline Service Center. As an example, she said some lawmakers mentioned hoping to examine how Hong Kong's "1823" service could better serve the public, and the Chief Executive has agreed to and acknowledged the lawmakers' visit to "1823." House Committee Chairman Chan Chun-ying later added that Beijing's "12345" service center integrates the resources of various departments, with targets and follow-up mechanisms, so that when citizens call, their problems can be resolved thoroughly. Hong Kong's "1823" hotline, by contrast, mainly refers inquiries to other departments, and information from the visit will be provided to the government.

Multiple lawmakers full of praise

When meeting the media, several lawmakers were full of praise for the exchange session, describing it as candid and allowing them to speak from the heart, while also chiming in to emphasize cooperation between the executive and legislative branches.

Chan Hoi-yan described the exchange as "very sincere and very candid," saying that views that were harder to express in the past could be discussed in a warm and in-depth manner at the session. She gave an example: in the past, when policies reached the legislature, they were often already "a fait accompli," leaving little room for discussion, and lawmakers were unable to make changes based on public views, so the result "may not be as ideal as we hope." She hoped there could be ample time before policies are introduced to brief lawmakers. She said the Chief Executive was very understanding and respectful on this point, and she felt his sincerity. She hopes to secure more time to communicate with lawmakers and hear their reflection of public sentiment, though she also understands that "not every policy can have such ample lead time." Chan hoped that through this dialogue, the relationship between the executive and legislative branches would be closer, describing the two sides as "close comrades-in-arms, a single team," and saying that as long as they work together, they can certainly resolve livelihood challenges.

Priscilla Leung also said that having served as a lawmaker for multiple terms, "this is the first time I felt the Chief Executive communicating with Legislative Council members in such an amiable and sincere manner," and that she could see the government and the Chief Executive were addressing the public's urgent concerns. She shared her views on issues such as community governance and the development of the Northern Metropolis during the session. When asked whether more unrestricted discussions should be added in the future to replace formal proceedings, Leung, who also chairs the Committee on Rules of Procedure, quipped that such rule-free discussions "were very effective," and that "if time permits, we should do it together often."

House Committee Chairman Chan Chun-ying described the atmosphere as very relaxed and free from language restrictions, with lawmakers communicating in Cantonese, English, and Putonghua. He believed all lawmakers would consider this format more relaxed and conducive to speaking from the heart than the formal use of official languages in council proceedings. Chow Ho-ding also described the exchange as candid and reiterated that in the executive and legislative branches, "we are one team, playing the match together."
